shortQuestions: During a war the boys were being evacuated from Britain by plane; the plane was shot down/crashed on an uninhabited tropical island, and the boys survived with no adults.
Ralph found a large conch shell in the lagoon and, with Piggy's help, blew it like a trumpet; the loud sound called all the scattered boys together to one place for a meeting.

Jack and his choir boys came marching along the beach in two lines, dressed in black cloaks and caps with silver badges, looking like a strange dark creature in the heat; Jack, tall and red-haired, led them with authority and they halted in order before the assembly.
The first issue was choosing a leader. They held a vote; Ralph, who had the conch, was elected chief, while Jack was given charge of his choir as hunters to satisfy him.
Ralph believed they would be rescued if they kept a signal fire burning on the mountain so that a passing ship would see the smoke; he also hoped his father, a naval officer, would come for them.
The rule was that whoever held the conch had the right to speak in the meeting and others must listen; it was made to keep order, give everyone a fair chance and make the assemblies democratic.

In the hallucination scene Simon, alone in the forest, imagines the pig's head on the stick (the Lord of the Flies) speaking to him. It tells him that the 'beast' is not outside but inside the boys themselves. The scene reveals the novel's main idea about the evil within human nature.

'Lord of the Flies' is a translation of 'Beelzebub', a name of the devil. It refers to the pig's head on a stick swarming with flies, which the boys offer to the beast. The title symbolises the evil and savagery that exist within human beings.
Roger rolls a huge rock that kills Piggy and shatters the conch into pieces. It suggests the complete end of order, reason and civilisation on the island and the victory of savagery.
Jack's tribe sets the island on fire while hunting Ralph. The smoke attracts a passing naval ship; an officer lands on the beach just as Ralph falls at his feet, and the boys are rescued.

Ralph's priorities were order, building shelters, keeping the signal fire and being rescued. Jack cared only about hunting, meat, power and fun; he ignored the fire and rules, which led to the split between them.
Simon represents natural goodness and spiritual insight — he is kind, helpful and thoughtful, and he understands that the beast is within the boys; some critics see him as a Christ-like figure.

Both Ralph and Piggy stand for order and civilisation. Ralph is athletic, attractive and a natural leader, but less intelligent; Piggy is fat, asthmatic and short-sighted, mocked by others, but he is the most intelligent and logical. Ralph provides leadership, Piggy provides ideas.

The mock-hunts show how the boys' games gradually become real violence; chanting "Kill the pig!" they lose control, attack Robert and later kill Simon — showing the growth of savagery in human nature.

These are Jack's words. On the occasion of his feast after leaving Ralph's group, he invites the boys to join his tribe, promising them meat, hunting and protection from the beast — he is trying to win followers away from Ralph.

At the feast Jack sits like an idol, painted and garlanded, with power resting on his shoulders. Golding shows that Jack has now become a tyrant ruler; his authority comes from fear and the boys' desire for meat and excitement, not from law or reason.

These are Ralph's words. The statement is true in the story: the fire is the boys' only link with civilisation and hope of rescue; when they neglect it, they lose that hope, and ironically it is a fire (the burning island) that finally brings rescue.

The dominant theme is the conflict between civilisation and savagery — the instinct to live by rules and morality versus the instinct to seek power and violence. Without the restraints of society, the evil within human nature comes out.
The novel suggests that children are not naturally innocent; they have the same capacity for cruelty, fear and lust for power as adults, and without guidance and rules they can easily turn savage.

Symbols: the conch shell — order, democracy and authority; Piggy's glasses — intelligence, science and reason (also the means of making fire); the signal fire — hope of rescue and link with civilisation; the beast — the evil and fear inside human beings.

The conch shell symbolises law and democratic order; Piggy's glasses stand for reason and the power of science; the signal fire stands for hope and the connection with civilisation (when it goes out, hope fades); the beast represents the inner evil and savagery of mankind, which the boys wrongly think is outside them.

s: 1. Character sketches — Ralph: elected leader, fair, sensible, stands for order and rescue; he weakens as savagery grows but keeps his humanity. Jack: proud, aggressive head of the choir who becomes a cruel dictator; he represents the lust for power and savagery. Piggy: intelligent, practical, short-sighted and weak; represents reason and science; mocked and finally killed. Simon: quiet, kind and spiritual; understands the true nature of the beast; killed by the boys in a frenzy.

2. Ralph and Jack compared: both are natural leaders, but Ralph leads by consent and rules while Jack rules by fear and force; Ralph wants shelter, fire and rescue, Jack wants hunting, meat and power; Ralph represents civilisation, Jack represents savagery.

activities: Role-play guide: the 'Ralph group' proposes order-based solutions (rules, sharing work, keeping the fire, holding meetings with the conch); the 'Jack group' proposes force-based solutions (hunting, a strong leader, punishment). After presenting proposals, the class discusses which approach better solves problems and why democratic order is essential.
